fields.value: The paper frames its focus as joint attention in HRI and proposes TOP-JAM to represent and track joint-attention states from behavioral data. It describes social attention as a continuum of individual attention and four states with increasing jointness: monitoring, common, mutual, and shared.

fields.value: The paper presents joint attention as supporting coordination, sharing, understanding, cooperation, shared goals, and rapport. TOP-JAM is intended to provide JA-state estimates that can support robot interaction skills such as initiating, responding to, or ensuring joint attention.

quotes.text: Hence, JA is essential for coordinating, sharing, understanding and cooperating with others ([8], [9], [10], [11]).
This skill is crucial for the accomplishment of shared goals through joint action ([5], [6]), and constitutes the basis for establishing rapport in HRI (e.g. in [7]).

We believe that TOP-JAM is a representation general enough to be integrated to several HRI tasks and scenarios, providing valuable information for ensuring robot interaction skills such as initiating, responding or ensuring JA [14].

fields.value: TOP-JAM estimates pairwise attention states from behavioral inputs including head position and direction, torso position and yaw, hand position, object position and properties, and speaking probability. It uses continuous attractor neural networks and logical feature operations; experimental behavior was controlled in closed loop, and observations were captured with motion tracking. Speech recognition was simulated because it was not operational during the experiment.

quotes.text: Due to differences in the body morphology of humans and the humanoid Pepper, behavior data from the robot was captured both from external markers fixed to its body to determine absolute position, combined with the computation of the direct geometric model to determine the head direction.

fields.value: The paper presents TOP-JAM, a neural-network model for representing and tracking joint attention in interactions involving multiple humans and robots. In a lab experiment with two people and Pepper, it tracked pairwise attention states with stable estimates; the paper also reports simulation computation times.

RQ1; RQ2; RQ4; RQ5; RQ6 — The paper characterizes joint attention through a scale of individual and social attention states, describes its roles in coordination and cooperation, and details the model and sensing used to estimate it. It studies the model with two humans and a Pepper robot, including how Pepper’s morphology shaped behavior-data capture.
